fp1_series_power_sums.description: Read inclusive sigma limits and derive the standard sums of integers, squares and cubes from consecutive differences.

sections.title: What does each limit in sigma notation mean?
sections.label: Read inclusive limits
sections.intro: The index runs through every integer from the lower limit through the upper limit. A summand is the expression evaluated at one index.

blocks.html: The count from p to q is \(q-p+1\). To use a standard sum beginning at one, subtract the part ending immediately before p.

blocks.title: Read the limits before counting the terms
blocks.prompt: Find the number of terms in \(\sum_{r=3}^{8}r\) and evaluate the sum.
blocks.hint: Both endpoint indices contribute, so the count includes one extra.
blocks.solution:
The indices start at \(3\) and end at \(8\), inclusive, so the count is \(6\).

Use the sum from one to the upper end, then subtract the sum up to \(2\).

This gives \(33\).

blocks.html: The upper index is not the number of terms when the starting index is greater than one.

sections.title: How do squared differences give the sum of integers?
sections.label: Sum the difference of squares
sections.intro: A difference of consecutive squares simplifies to a linear expression. Sum it across the whole range.

blocks.html: \((r+1)^2-r^2=2r+1\) gives a telescoping left side. The right side has twice the desired sum and one copy of one for each index.

blocks.title: Isolate a power from a difference of consecutive powers
blocks.prompt: Sum \(- r^{2} + \left(r + 1\right)^{2}=2 r + 1\) for \(r=1,\ldots,5\). Find the sum of its left-hand side and hence \(\sum_{r=1}^{5}r\).
blocks.hint: Write the first and last differences, then identify which interior values cancel.
blocks.solution:
Consecutive powers cancel on the left, leaving \((6)^{2}-1=35\) as the boundary difference.

The right side is \(2 r + 1\) for each term. Summing its terms below degree \(1\) gives \(5\).

The largest power has multiplier \(2\). Subtract the lower-power total then divide by this multiplier to get \(15\).

blocks.html: Remember to subtract the constant contributions before dividing by two.

sections.title: How can I derive the sum of squares?
sections.label: Isolate the square coefficient
sections.intro: The difference of cubes gives an expression whose largest power is a square. The remaining linear and constant totals are already known.

blocks.html: \((r+1)^3-r^3=3r^2+3r+1\). Sum from one to n and retain only the first and last cubes on the left.

blocks.title: Isolate a power from a difference of consecutive powers
blocks.prompt: Sum \(- r^{3} + \left(r + 1\right)^{3}=3 r^{2} + 3 r + 1\) for \(r=1,\ldots,5\). Find the sum of its left-hand side and hence \(\sum_{r=1}^{5}r^{2}\).
blocks.hint: Write the first and last differences, then identify which interior values cancel.
blocks.solution:
Consecutive powers cancel on the left, leaving \((6)^{3}-1=215\) as the boundary difference.

The right side is \(3 r^{2} + 3 r + 1\) for each term. Summing its terms below degree \(2\) gives \(50\).

The largest power has multiplier \(3\). Subtract the lower-power total then divide by this multiplier to get \(55\).

blocks.html: The final positive cube is at \(n+1\), not at n.

blocks.title: Isolate a power from a difference of consecutive powers
blocks.prompt: Sum \(- r^{3} + \left(r + 1\right)^{3}=3 r^{2} + 3 r + 1\) for \(r=1,\ldots,7\). Find the sum of its left-hand side and hence \(\sum_{r=1}^{7}r^{2}\).
blocks.hint: Write the first and last differences, then identify which interior values cancel.
blocks.solution:
Consecutive powers cancel on the left, leaving \((8)^{3}-1=511\) as the boundary difference.

The right side is \(3 r^{2} + 3 r + 1\) for each term. Summing its terms below degree \(2\) gives \(91\).

The largest power has multiplier \(3\). Subtract the lower-power total then divide by this multiplier to get \(140\).

sections.title: Why does the fourth-power difference produce cubes?
sections.label: Use the highest surviving power
sections.intro: When expanding a difference of consecutive powers, the top power cancels. The binomial coefficient of the next term determines the multiplier.

blocks.html: \((r+1)^4-r^4=4r^3+6r^2+4r+1\). Use the previously known totals before isolating the sum of cubes.

blocks.title: Isolate a power from a difference of consecutive powers
blocks.prompt: Sum \(- r^{4} + \left(r + 1\right)^{4}=4 r^{3} + 6 r^{2} + 4 r + 1\) for \(r=1,\ldots,5\). Find the sum of its left-hand side and hence \(\sum_{r=1}^{5}r^{3}\).
blocks.hint: Write the first and last differences, then identify which interior values cancel.
blocks.solution:
Consecutive powers cancel on the left, leaving \((6)^{4}-1=1295\) as the boundary difference.

The right side is \(4 r^{3} + 6 r^{2} + 4 r + 1\) for each term. Summing its terms below degree \(3\) gives \(395\).

The largest power has multiplier \(4\). Subtract the lower-power total then divide by this multiplier to get \(225\).

blocks.html: Keep the square and linear contributions as separate sums, with their original coefficients.

sections.title: Can a cube sum telescope directly?
sections.label: Compare consecutive squared totals
sections.intro: The square of a triangular total can itself be treated as a function of the last index.

blocks.html: \(A_r=\left(\frac{r(r+1)}2\right)^2\) satisfies \(A_r-A_{r-1}=r^3\). Use a difference of squares to show it.

blocks.title: Derive a cube sum from successive triangular squares
blocks.prompt: Define \(A_r=\frac{r^{2} \left(r + 1\right)^{2}}{4}\). Find \(A_r-A_{r-1}\) as a polynomial in \(r\) and evaluate \(\sum_{r=2}^{5}r^{3}\).
blocks.hint: Use a difference of squares and keep the correct first boundary.
blocks.solution:
Factor the difference as \(\frac{r^2}{4}\big((r+1)^2-(r-1)^2\big)\).

The bracket simplifies to \(4r\), so the difference is \(r^3\).

Sum from two. Only \(A_5-A_1\) remains, giving \(224\).

blocks.html: This identity is between successive values of A. It is not a claim that sums usually commute with squaring.

blocks.title: Derive a cube sum from successive triangular squares
blocks.prompt: Define \(A_r=\frac{r^{2} \left(r + 1\right)^{2}}{4}\). Find \(A_r-A_{r-1}\) as a polynomial in \(r\) and evaluate \(\sum_{r=2}^{7}r^{3}\).
blocks.hint: Use a difference of squares and keep the correct first boundary.
blocks.solution:
Factor the difference as \(\frac{r^2}{4}\big((r+1)^2-(r-1)^2\big)\).

The bracket simplifies to \(4r\), so the difference is \(r^3\).

Sum from two. Only \(A_7-A_1\) remains, giving \(783\).

solution: The indices start at \(2\) and end at \(6\), inclusive, so the count is \(5\).
Use the sum from one to the upper end, then subtract the sum up to \(1\).
This gives \(20\).

The right side is \(2 r + 1\) for each term. Summing its terms below degree \(1\) gives \(4\).

solution: Consecutive powers cancel on the left, leaving \((5)^{3}-1=124\) as the boundary difference.

examples.title: Isolate a power from a difference of consecutive powers
examples.question: Sum \(- r^{4} + \left(r + 1\right)^{4}=4 r^{3} + 6 r^{2} + 4 r + 1\) for \(r=1,\ldots,4\). Find the sum of its left-hand side and hence \(\sum_{r=1}^{4}r^{3}\).
solution: Consecutive powers cancel on the left, leaving \((5)^{4}-1=624\) as the boundary difference.

solution: Factor the difference as \(\frac{r^2}{4}\big((r+1)^2-(r-1)^2\big)\).

glossary.definition: The expression being added at one index.
The integer variable in the sum.
Both listed endpoints occur in the sum.
A value at the next index minus the one at this index.
A term left when interior terms have cancelled.

revision.body:

SituationMethod
\(\sum_{r=1}^{n}r\)\(\frac{n(n+1)}2\)

related.title: Using power sums and finite limits

fp1_series_finite_sums.description: Use standard sums on polynomial, shifted and alternating ranges. Recover terms and blocks from partial sums.

sections.title: When should I expand a summand before using the formulae?
sections.label: Separate powers
sections.intro: Standard results cover constants, integers, squares and cubes. Expand a polynomial summand to express it as a linear combination of these parts.

blocks.html: The sum of a linear combination is the same combination of the separate sums with the same index limits.

blocks.title: Expand the summand before using standard results
blocks.prompt: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r + 5\right) \left(3 r - 1\right)\) as a polynomial in \(n\).
blocks.hint: Multiplying two separate sums would count terms with different indices.
blocks.solution:
Expand to \(3 r^{2} + 14 r - 5\).

Sum the quadratic and linear terms separately and count \(n\) copies of the constant.

Combine the standard results to obtain \(n^{3} + \frac{17 n^{2}}{2} + \frac{5 n}{2}\).

blocks.html: Do not multiply two standard sums to reproduce the sum of products at matching indices.

sections.title: Which partial sum do I subtract for a later range?
sections.label: Stop just before the first retained index
sections.intro: The partial sum to the upper index also includes earlier terms. Subtract precisely the terms that occur before the requested start.

blocks.html: For a block from p to q inclusive use \(S_q-S_{p-1}\) after substituting the actual expressions for both limits.

blocks.title: Subtract the sum before the lower limit
blocks.prompt: Find the number of terms and the value of \(\sum_{r=n+1}^{2 n + 1}\left(3 r + 5\right)\) as polynomials in \(n\).

fields.label: Term count as a polynomial in n
Sum as a polynomial in n

blocks.hint: The lower limit is included, so subtract only the terms before it.
blocks.solution:
The term count is upper index minus lower index plus one, giving \(n + 1\).

Subtract the sum up to \(n\) from the sum up to \(2 n + 1\).

The result is \(\frac{9 n^{2}}{2} + \frac{25 n}{2} + 8\).

blocks.html: Subtracting the sum through p also deletes the first term you were meant to include.

sections.title: How do I handle the two parities in an alternating sum?
sections.label: Pair successive terms
sections.intro: An even number of terms groups into adjacent pairs. An odd number leaves one unpaired term at the end.

blocks.html: Simplify the difference within a pair first and then use standard sums for the pair index.

blocks.title: Pair an alternating sum, then handle a leftover term
blocks.prompt: Let \(A_m=\sum_{r=1}^{m}(-1)^{r-1}\left(r + 3\right)^2\). Find \(A_{2n}\) and \(A_{2n+1}\) as polynomials in \(n\).
blocks.hint: Use adjacent pairs first. For an odd upper index include one extra positive term.
blocks.solution:
An adjacent pair is the odd-index term minus the even-index term. For pair \(r\) this simplifies to \(- 4 r - 5\).

There are \(n\) complete pairs, giving \(A_{2n}=- 2 n^{2} - 7 n\).

The next unpaired term has positive sign. Adding it gives \(A_{2n+1}=2 n^{2} + 9 n + 16\).

blocks.html: The index of a pair is not the index of either of its members. Use consecutive lower and upper indices carefully.

blocks.title: Pair an alternating sum, then handle a leftover term
blocks.prompt: Let \(A_m=\sum_{r=1}^{m}(-1)^{r-1}\left(r + 5\right)^2\). Find \(A_{2n}\) and \(A_{2n+1}\) as polynomials in \(n\).
blocks.hint: Use adjacent pairs first. For an odd upper index include one extra positive term.
blocks.solution:
An adjacent pair is the odd-index term minus the even-index term. For pair \(r\) this simplifies to \(- 4 r - 9\).

There are \(n\) complete pairs, giving \(A_{2n}=- 2 n^{2} - 11 n\).

The next unpaired term has positive sign. Adding it gives \(A_{2n+1}=2 n^{2} + 13 n + 36\).

sections.title: Why do consecutive partial sums reveal a single term?
sections.label: Subtract the sum one term earlier
sections.intro: Let \(S_n\) be the total of the first n terms. Its predecessor includes all those terms except the nth.

blocks.html: Use \(u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\) for a single term, or the difference of two partial sums for a whole block.

blocks.title: Recover a term and a later block from a partial sum
blocks.prompt: The partial sum is \(S_n=n \left(n + 3\right) \left(2 n + 5\right)\). Find \(u_n\) and \(\sum_{r=n+1}^{2n}u_r\) as polynomials in \(n\).
blocks.hint: A partial sum and a single term are different quantities. Subtract adjacent partial sums to isolate one term.
blocks.solution:
The nth term is \(S_n-S_{n-1}\). Subtracting yields \(u_n=6 n^{2} + 16 n + 6\).

The later block uses \(S_{2n}-S_n\), since the term at n is not in the block.

Simplify to \(14 n^{3} + 33 n^{2} + 15 n\).

blocks.html: A formula for \(S_n\) does not usually give the nth term on its own.

sections.title: Which terms do I keep when a shifted square is expanded?
sections.label: Use the linear cross term
sections.intro: A square of a shifted linear expression contributes one term of each degree from zero to two.

blocks.html: Expand \((ar+b)^2=a^2r^2+2abr+b^2\) first. In each standard sum keep the coefficients outside.

blocks.title: Separate the middle term of a shifted square
blocks.prompt: Find the coefficient of \(r\) when \(\left(3 r + 5\right)^{2}\) is expanded, then find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(3 r + 5\right)^{2}\) as a polynomial in \(n\).
blocks.hint: Use all three terms of the binomial expansion.
blocks.solution:
The expansion includes \(2ab=30\) as the coefficient of \(r\).

Use separate formulae for squares, first powers and constants. The constant is added \(n\) times.

The sum simplifies to \(3 n^{3} + \frac{39 n^{2}}{2} + \frac{83 n}{2}\).

blocks.html: The constant contributes once per index, and the cross term contributes an entire first-power sum.

blocks.title: Separate the middle term of a shifted square
blocks.prompt: Find the coefficient of \(r\) when \(\left(5 r + 9\right)^{2}\) is expanded, then find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(5 r + 9\right)^{2}\) as a polynomial in \(n\).
blocks.hint: Use all three terms of the binomial expansion.
blocks.solution:
The expansion includes \(2ab=90\) as the coefficient of \(r\).

Use separate formulae for squares, first powers and constants. The constant is added \(n\) times.

The sum simplifies to \(\frac{25 n^{3}}{3} + \frac{115 n^{2}}{2} + \frac{781 n}{6}\).

examples.title: Expand the summand before using standard results
examples.question: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r + 3\right) \left(2 r - 1\right)\) as a polynomial in \(n\).
solution: Sum the quadratic and linear terms separately and count \(n\) copies of the constant.
Combine the standard results to obtain \(\frac{2 n^{3}}{3} + \frac{7 n^{2}}{2} - \frac{n}{6}\).

examples.title: Subtract the sum before the lower limit
examples.question: Find the number of terms and the value of \(\sum_{r=n+1}^{2 n}\left(2 r + 3\right)\) as polynomials in \(n\).
solution: The term count is upper index minus lower index plus one, giving \(n\).
Subtract the sum up to \(n\) from the sum up to \(2 n\).
The result is \(3 n^{2} + 4 n\).

examples.title: Pair an alternating sum, then handle a leftover term
examples.question: Let \(A_m=\sum_{r=1}^{m}(-1)^{r-1}\left(r + 2\right)^2\). Find \(A_{2n}\) and \(A_{2n+1}\) as polynomials in \(n\).
solution: An adjacent pair is the odd-index term minus the even-index term. For pair \(r\) this simplifies to \(- 4 r - 3\).
There are \(n\) complete pairs, giving \(A_{2n}=- 2 n^{2} - 5 n\).
The next unpaired term has positive sign. Adding it gives \(A_{2n+1}=2 n^{2} + 7 n + 9\).

examples.title: Pair an alternating sum, then handle a leftover term
examples.question: Let \(A_m=\sum_{r=1}^{m}(-1)^{r-1}\left(r + 4\right)^2\). Find \(A_{2n}\) and \(A_{2n+1}\) as polynomials in \(n\).
solution: An adjacent pair is the odd-index term minus the even-index term. For pair \(r\) this simplifies to \(- 4 r - 7\).
There are \(n\) complete pairs, giving \(A_{2n}=- 2 n^{2} - 9 n\).
The next unpaired term has positive sign. Adding it gives \(A_{2n+1}=2 n^{2} + 11 n + 25\).

examples.title: Recover a term and a later block from a partial sum
examples.question: The partial sum is \(S_n=n \left(n + 2\right) \left(2 n + 3\right)\). Find \(u_n\) and \(\sum_{r=n+1}^{2n}u_r\) as polynomials in \(n\).
solution: The nth term is \(S_n-S_{n-1}\). Subtracting yields \(u_n=6 n^{2} + 8 n + 1\).
The later block uses \(S_{2n}-S_n\), since the term at n is not in the block.

examples.title: Separate the middle term of a shifted square
examples.question: Find the coefficient of \(r\) when \(\left(2 r + 3\right)^{2}\) is expanded, then find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(2 r + 3\right)^{2}\) as a polynomial in \(n\).
solution: The expansion includes \(2ab=12\) as the coefficient of \(r\).
Use separate formulae for squares, first powers and constants. The constant is added \(n\) times.
The sum simplifies to \(\frac{4 n^{3}}{3} + 8 n^{2} + \frac{47 n}{3}\).

examples.title: Separate the middle term of a shifted square
examples.question: Find the coefficient of \(r\) when \(\left(4 r + 7\right)^{2}\) is expanded, then find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(4 r + 7\right)^{2}\) as a polynomial in \(n\).
solution: The expansion includes \(2ab=56\) as the coefficient of \(r\).
Use separate formulae for squares, first powers and constants. The constant is added \(n\) times.
The sum simplifies to \(\frac{16 n^{3}}{3} + 36 n^{2} + \frac{239 n}{3}\).

Simplify to \(14 n^{3} + 45 n^{2} + 28 n\).

extraPractice.title: Separate the middle term of a shifted square
extraPractice.prompt: Find the coefficient of \(r\) when \(\left(6 r + 11\right)^{2}\) is expanded, then find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(6 r + 11\right)^{2}\) as a polynomial in \(n\).
extraPractice.hint: Use all three terms of the binomial expansion.
extraPractice.solution:
The expansion includes \(2ab=132\) as the coefficient of \(r\).

Use separate formulae for squares, first powers and constants. The constant is added \(n\) times.

The sum simplifies to \(12 n^{3} + 84 n^{2} + 193 n\).

Consecutive terms between two given limits.
Successive terms have alternating plus and minus multipliers.
Grouping each odd-index term with the next even-index term.

fp1_series_differences.description: Expose cancelling terms using partial fractions and other differences, then account for every surviving endpoint.

sections.title: Why do adjacent terms cancel?
sections.label: Write the first and final differences
sections.intro: When a term is one value minus its successor, the successor appears again with positive sign in the next term.

blocks.html: The finite sum of \(F(r)-F(r+1)\) from p to q leaves \(F(p)-F(q+1)\).

blocks.title: Write a partial fraction as a one-step difference
blocks.prompt: Let \(u_r=\frac{1}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right)}\). Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{5}u_r\).
blocks.hint: Write the first two and final pair terms before cancelling.
blocks.solution:
Decompose the term as \(- \frac{3}{3 r + 6} + \frac{3}{3 r + 3}\). Verify by using the common denominator.

The negative fraction of each term cancels the next positive fraction.

Keep \(\frac{1}{2}\) from the first term and subtract \(\frac{1}{7}\) from the last, giving \(\frac{5}{14}\).

blocks.html: The final negative term has index one more than the upper summation endpoint.

sections.title: How many terms survive when the shift is larger than one?
sections.label: Compare boundary groups
sections.intro: Two terms separated by more than one index cancel further apart in the list. The missing partners leave several terms at each end.

blocks.html: For a shift of d, compare the two full index ranges. Keep each unpaired positive and negative term.

blocks.title: Keep as many boundary terms as the shift
blocks.prompt: Find the sum of \(u_r=\frac{9}{\left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 6\right)}\) from \(r=1\) to \(5\).
blocks.hint: A shift of more than one leaves more than one term at each end.
blocks.solution:
Split the fraction into \(- \frac{3}{r + 6} + \frac{3}{r + 3}\). The difference has a shift of \(3\).

The first \(3\) positive terms survive and sum to \(\frac{37}{20}\). The last \(3\) negative terms have total magnitude \(\frac{299}{330}\).

Subtract the two boundary totals for \(\frac{623}{660}\).

blocks.html: Cancelling only a first and last term loses entire boundary groups when the shift exceeds one.

sections.title: Can three factors telescope without decomposing into three fractions?
sections.label: Try two shifted two-factor fractions
sections.intro: A product of three consecutive linear factors may be the common denominator of two simpler terms.

blocks.html: Look for two adjacent two-factor denominators sharing the middle factor. Subtract and verify the original numerator.

blocks.title: Spot a difference of two simpler products
blocks.prompt: Calculate \(\sum_{r=1}^{5}\frac{6}{\left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right) \left(r + 5\right)}\).
blocks.hint: Start with fractions whose denominators match at the next index.
blocks.solution:
Keep the middle linear factor in both simpler fractions. Their difference is \(- \frac{3}{\left(r + 4\right) \left(r + 5\right)} + \frac{3}{\left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\).

Bringing this expression over one denominator recovers the given summand.

The sum telescopes to \(\frac{7}{60}\).

blocks.html: The difference of the two remaining linear expressions may introduce a fixed multiplier. Keep it.

blocks.title: Spot a difference of two simpler products
blocks.prompt: Calculate \(\sum_{r=1}^{7}\frac{10}{\left(r + 5\right) \left(r + 6\right) \left(r + 7\right)}\).
blocks.hint: Start with fractions whose denominators match at the next index.
blocks.solution:
Keep the middle linear factor in both simpler fractions. Their difference is \(- \frac{5}{\left(r + 6\right) \left(r + 7\right)} + \frac{5}{\left(r + 5\right) \left(r + 6\right)}\).

Bringing this expression over one denominator recovers the given summand.

The sum telescopes to \(\frac{25}{273}\).

sections.title: What if a geometric factor is part of the cancelling expression?
sections.label: Move the full term together
sections.intro: A function F can contain both a geometric multiplier and a rational term. The whole expression shifts its index.

blocks.html: Find the endpoint values by substituting into every occurrence of the index in F.

blocks.title: Keep a geometric factor together with its index
blocks.hint: Treat F as a complete expression. The last index is one beyond the upper summation index.
blocks.solution:
The successive term is \(\frac{3^{- r - 1}}{r + 4}\). The exponent and reciprocal both advance by one.

Every interior \(F(r)\) cancels with its occurrence in the previous difference.

The last negative term is \(F(6)\). The total is \(\frac{1}{12}\) minus \(\frac{1}{6561}\), giving \(\frac{2183}{26244}\).

blocks.html: Changing the reciprocal index while leaving the exponential unchanged can prevent the cancellation.

sections.title: How do logarithms produce a difference?
sections.label: Use the quotient law
sections.intro: A logarithm of a positive ratio becomes the difference of the logarithms of its positive numerator and denominator.

blocks.html: Check positivity of the arguments. Then compare neighbouring numerator and denominator terms and keep the uncancelled logs.

blocks.title: Rewrite logarithms so the arguments telescope
blocks.prompt: Express \(\sum_{r=1}^{5}\ln\left(\frac{r+4}{r+3}\right)\) as \(\ln A\). Give the exact argument \(A\).
blocks.hint: Use the quotient law and cancel the interior logarithms before combining the endpoints.
blocks.solution:
Split each logarithm into the log of the numerator minus the log of the denominator. All arguments are positive.

Successive logarithms cancel. The last numerator is \(9\) and the first denominator is \(4\).

Combine the two remaining logarithms to obtain \(\ln\left(\frac{9}{4}\right)\).

blocks.html: Taking the logarithm of a difference does not produce a difference of logarithms.

blocks.title: Rewrite logarithms so the arguments telescope
blocks.prompt: Express \(\sum_{r=1}^{7}\ln\left(\frac{r+6}{r+5}\right)\) as \(\ln A\). Give the exact argument \(A\).
blocks.hint: Use the quotient law and cancel the interior logarithms before combining the endpoints.
blocks.solution:
Split each logarithm into the log of the numerator minus the log of the denominator. All arguments are positive.

Successive logarithms cancel. The last numerator is \(13\) and the first denominator is \(6\).

Combine the two remaining logarithms to obtain \(\ln\left(\frac{13}{6}\right)\).

examples.title: Write a partial fraction as a one-step difference
examples.question: Let \(u_r=\frac{4}{\left(2 r + 1\right) \left(2 r + 3\right)}\). Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{4}u_r\).
solution: Decompose the term as \(- \frac{2}{2 r + 3} + \frac{2}{2 r + 1}\). Verify by using the common denominator.
The negative fraction of each term cancels the next positive fraction.
Keep \(\frac{2}{3}\) from the first term and subtract \(\frac{2}{11}\) from the last, giving \(\frac{16}{33}\).

examples.title: Keep as many boundary terms as the shift
examples.question: Find the sum of \(u_r=\frac{4}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\) from \(r=1\) to \(4\).
solution: Split the fraction into \(- \frac{2}{r + 4} + \frac{2}{r + 2}\). The difference has a shift of \(2\).
The first \(2\) positive terms survive and sum to \(\frac{7}{6}\). The last \(2\) negative terms have total magnitude \(\frac{15}{28}\).
Subtract the two boundary totals for \(\frac{53}{84}\).

examples.title: Spot a difference of two simpler products
examples.question: Calculate \(\sum_{r=1}^{4}\frac{4}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\).
solution: Keep the middle linear factor in both simpler fractions. Their difference is \(- \frac{2}{\left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)} + \frac{2}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right)}\).
Bringing this expression over one denominator recovers the given summand.
The sum telescopes to \(\frac{11}{84}\).

examples.title: Spot a difference of two simpler products
examples.question: Calculate \(\sum_{r=1}^{6}\frac{8}{\left(r + 4\right) \left(r + 5\right) \left(r + 6\right)}\).
solution: Keep the middle linear factor in both simpler fractions. Their difference is \(- \frac{4}{\left(r + 5\right) \left(r + 6\right)} + \frac{4}{\left(r + 4\right) \left(r + 5\right)}\).
Bringing this expression over one denominator recovers the given summand.
The sum telescopes to \(\frac{17}{165}\).

examples.title: Keep a geometric factor together with its index
examples.question: Using \(F(r)=\frac{2^{- r}}{r + 2}\), find \(\sum_{r=1}^{4}F(r)-F(r+1)\).
solution: The successive term is \(\frac{2^{- r - 1}}{r + 3}\). The exponent and reciprocal both advance by one.
Every interior \(F(r)\) cancels with its occurrence in the previous difference.
The last negative term is \(F(5)\). The total is \(\frac{1}{6}\) minus \(\frac{1}{224}\), giving \(\frac{109}{672}\).

examples.title: Rewrite logarithms so the arguments telescope
examples.question: Express \(\sum_{r=1}^{4}\ln\left(\frac{r+3}{r+2}\right)\) as \(\ln A\). Give the exact argument \(A\).
solution: Split each logarithm into the log of the numerator minus the log of the denominator. All arguments are positive.
Successive logarithms cancel. The last numerator is \(7\) and the first denominator is \(3\).
Combine the two remaining logarithms to obtain \(\ln\left(\frac{7}{3}\right)\).

examples.title: Rewrite logarithms so the arguments telescope
examples.question: Express \(\sum_{r=1}^{6}\ln\left(\frac{r+5}{r+4}\right)\) as \(\ln A\). Give the exact argument \(A\).
solution: Split each logarithm into the log of the numerator minus the log of the denominator. All arguments are positive.
Successive logarithms cancel. The last numerator is \(11\) and the first denominator is \(5\).
Combine the two remaining logarithms to obtain \(\ln\left(\frac{11}{5}\right)\).

extraPractice.title: Write a partial fraction as a one-step difference
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(u_r=\frac{16}{\left(4 r + 5\right) \left(4 r + 9\right)}\). Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{6}u_r\).
extraPractice.hint: Write the first two and final pair terms before cancelling.
extraPractice.solution:
Decompose the term as \(- \frac{4}{4 r + 9} + \frac{4}{4 r + 5}\). Verify by using the common denominator.

The negative fraction of each term cancels the next positive fraction.

Keep \(\frac{4}{9}\) from the first term and subtract \(\frac{4}{33}\) from the last, giving \(\frac{32}{99}\).

extraPractice.title: Keep as many boundary terms as the shift
extraPractice.prompt: Find the sum of \(u_r=\frac{8}{\left(r + 4\right) \left(r + 6\right)}\) from \(r=1\) to \(6\).
extraPractice.hint: A shift of more than one leaves more than one term at each end.
extraPractice.solution:
Split the fraction into \(- \frac{4}{r + 6} + \frac{4}{r + 4}\). The difference has a shift of \(2\).

The first \(2\) positive terms survive and sum to \(\frac{22}{15}\). The last \(2\) negative terms have total magnitude \(\frac{23}{33}\).

Subtract the two boundary totals for \(\frac{127}{165}\).

extraPractice.title: Spot a difference of two simpler products
extraPractice.prompt: Calculate \(\sum_{r=1}^{8}\frac{12}{\left(r + 6\right) \left(r + 7\right) \left(r + 8\right)}\).
extraPractice.hint: Start with fractions whose denominators match at the next index.
extraPractice.solution:
Keep the middle linear factor in both simpler fractions. Their difference is \(- \frac{6}{\left(r + 7\right) \left(r + 8\right)} + \frac{6}{\left(r + 6\right) \left(r + 7\right)}\).

Bringing this expression over one denominator recovers the given summand.

The sum telescopes to \(\frac{23}{280}\).

extraPractice.title: Keep a geometric factor together with its index
extraPractice.hint: Treat F as a complete expression. The last index is one beyond the upper summation index.
extraPractice.solution:
The successive term is \(\frac{4^{- r - 1}}{r + 5}\). The exponent and reciprocal both advance by one.

Every interior \(F(r)\) cancels with its occurrence in the previous difference.

The last negative term is \(F(7)\). The total is \(\frac{1}{20}\) minus \(\frac{1}{180224}\), giving \(\frac{45051}{901120}\).

extraPractice.title: Rewrite logarithms so the arguments telescope
extraPractice.prompt: Express \(\sum_{r=1}^{8}\ln\left(\frac{r+7}{r+6}\right)\) as \(\ln A\). Give the exact argument \(A\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the quotient law and cancel the interior logarithms before combining the endpoints.
extraPractice.solution:
Split each logarithm into the log of the numerator minus the log of the denominator. All arguments are positive.

Successive logarithms cancel. The last numerator is \(15\) and the first denominator is \(7\).

Combine the two remaining logarithms to obtain \(\ln\left(\frac{15}{7}\right)\).

glossary.definition: A finite sum whose interior contributions cancel in pairs.
A sum of simpler rational terms giving the original fraction when combined.
Difference between the indices of cancelling copies of F.
A factor changing by the same multiplier at each index.
The log of a positive quotient is the difference of the logs.

related.title: Using power sums and finite limits

fp1_series_convergence.description: Find the sum to infinity from partial sums. Work with exact errors, strict cutoffs, exceptional parameters and moving blocks.

sections.title: What quantity must have a limit for a series to converge?
sections.label: Find the complete finite sum first
sections.intro: Convergence means that the sequence of complete partial sums approaches a finite number. A small individual term is not enough to establish that.

blocks.html: Find \(S_n\) before taking \(n\to\infty\). The exact remainder is \(S_\infty-S_n\) for a convergent series.

blocks.title: Subtract the finite sum from its limit
blocks.prompt: Find the sum to infinity of \(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{4}{\left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\) and the exact error after the first \(6\) terms.
blocks.hint: Keep the finite boundary until you have written the exact error.
blocks.solution:
The term telescopes as \(- \frac{4}{r + 4} + \frac{4}{r + 3}\), so \(S_n=1 - \frac{4}{n + 4}\).

The final reciprocal tends to zero. This leaves \(S_\infty=1\).

Subtracting \(S_n\) from this level gives \(\frac{4}{n + 4}\). At \(6\) terms the error is \(\frac{2}{5}\).

blocks.html: Taking a limit of the summand answers a different question from taking a limit of the sum.

sections.title: How do I find the first integer inside an error bound?
sections.label: Keep the direction and strictness
sections.intro: Use a formula for the difference from the limit. If it can have either sign, compare its magnitude with the tolerance.

blocks.html: For a positive decreasing remainder, solve the exact inequality and identify the first positive integer satisfying it.

blocks.title: Find the least integer that meets a strict cutoff
blocks.prompt: For the partial sums \(S_n=1 - \frac{4}{n + 4}\), find the least positive integer \(n\) for which the difference from the limit is strictly less than \(\frac{4}{13}\).
blocks.hint: An integer giving exact equality does not satisfy a strict inequality.
blocks.solution:
The limit is \(1\). The positive error is \(\frac{4}{n + 4}\).

At \(n=9\) the error equals the stated tolerance. The error then decreases strictly.

Equality is excluded, so the first accepted integer is \(10\).

blocks.html: If equality occurs at an integer and the bound is strict, the next integer is the first candidate.

sections.title: What if the last boundary does not tend to zero?
sections.label: Keep the full limiting level
sections.intro: A boundary term may contain both a vanishing part and a constant. Use the limit of the whole term.

blocks.html: For \(F(n+1)-F(1)\) take the limit of the varying part before subtracting the fixed initial value.

blocks.title: Keep the limiting value of a non-vanishing boundary
blocks.hint: Take the limit of the entire boundary term, including any constant part.
blocks.solution:
The finite sum is \(F(n+1)-F(1)\).

The upper term tends to \(2\), not to zero.

Subtract \(\frac{11}{4}\) for the infinite total \(- \frac{3}{4}\).

blocks.html: Do not drop a rational boundary merely because it contains a denominator growing with n. Compare numerator and denominator.

blocks.title: Keep the limiting value of a non-vanishing boundary
blocks.hint: Take the limit of the entire boundary term, including any constant part.
blocks.solution:
The finite sum is \(F(n+1)-F(1)\).

The upper term tends to \(4\), not to zero.

Subtract \(\frac{29}{6}\) for the infinite total \(- \frac{5}{6}\).

sections.title: When should I test parameter endpoints separately?
sections.label: Read the actual partial sum
sections.intro: A formula involving a geometric factor can degenerate at a parameter endpoint. Test the resulting partial sums directly.

blocks.html: Use the usual geometric limit when the magnitude of the ratio is less than one. Then inspect each boundary and any constant prefactor.

blocks.title: Check the degenerate geometric endpoint separately
blocks.prompt: For real \(q\) let \(u_r=q^r-q^{r+1}\). Give all values of \(q\) for which the series converges and give the infinite sum when \(q=- \frac{2}{3}\).

fields.label: Infinite sum for the stated q

blocks.hint: Use the explicit partial sum. Test both endpoints and keep any degenerate case.
blocks.solution:
The partial sum is \(q-q^{n+1}\). When \(|q|<1\) it tends to \(q\).

At \(q=1\) every term is zero, so it also converges. At \(q=-1\) the partial sums oscillate. For \(|q|>1\) their magnitudes grow without bound.

Thus the parameter interval is \(-1

blocks.html: A ratio test for one form cannot override a special value that makes every term zero.

sections.title: How can a shrinking block have a non-zero scaled limit?
sections.label: Scale the exact boundary expression
sections.intro: A block with both limits depending on n can shrink to zero even while its rescaled value approaches a non-zero number.

blocks.html: Write its exact telescoped expression, multiply by the requested scale and then divide by the leading power in each denominator.

blocks.title: Find a scaled limit of a block with moving endpoints
blocks.prompt: Let \(u_r=\frac{4}{\left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\). Find \(\lim_{n\to\infty}n\sum_{r=3 n + 1}^{5 n}u_r\).
blocks.hint: Determine the power of n in each boundary before taking the limit.
blocks.solution:
The block telescopes to \(\frac{4}{3 n + 4}\) minus \(\frac{4}{5 n + 4}\). Both terms tend to zero by themselves.

Multiply by \(n\) before taking limits. Divide each denominator by \(n\).

The result tends to \(\frac{4}{3}\) minus \(\frac{4}{5}\), so the limit is \(\frac{8}{15}\).

blocks.html: Taking the block limit first loses the rate of shrinkage and makes the later scaling invalid.

blocks.title: Find a scaled limit of a block with moving endpoints
blocks.prompt: Let \(u_r=\frac{6}{\left(r + 5\right) \left(r + 6\right)}\). Find \(\lim_{n\to\infty}n\sum_{r=5 n + 1}^{7 n}u_r\).
blocks.hint: Determine the power of n in each boundary before taking the limit.
blocks.solution:
The block telescopes to \(\frac{6}{5 n + 6}\) minus \(\frac{6}{7 n + 6}\). Both terms tend to zero by themselves.

Multiply by \(n\) before taking limits. Divide each denominator by \(n\).

The result tends to \(\frac{6}{5}\) minus \(\frac{6}{7}\), so the limit is \(\frac{12}{35}\).

examples.title: Subtract the finite sum from its limit
examples.question: Find the sum to infinity of \(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{3}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right)}\) and the exact error after the first \(5\) terms.
solution: The term telescopes as \(- \frac{3}{r + 3} + \frac{3}{r + 2}\), so \(S_n=1 - \frac{3}{n + 3}\).
The final reciprocal tends to zero. This leaves \(S_\infty=1\).
Subtracting \(S_n\) from this level gives \(\frac{3}{n + 3}\). At \(5\) terms the error is \(\frac{3}{8}\).

examples.title: Find the least integer that meets a strict cutoff
examples.question: For the partial sums \(S_n=1 - \frac{3}{n + 3}\), find the least positive integer \(n\) for which the difference from the limit is strictly less than \(\frac{3}{10}\).
solution: The limit is \(1\). The positive error is \(\frac{3}{n + 3}\).
At \(n=7\) the error equals the stated tolerance. The error then decreases strictly.
Equality is excluded, so the first accepted integer is \(8\).

examples.title: Keep the limiting value of a non-vanishing boundary
examples.question: Let \(F(r)=1 + \frac{2}{r + 2}\). Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}F(r+1)-F(r)\).
solution: The finite sum is \(F(n+1)-F(1)\).
The upper term tends to \(1\), not to zero.
Subtract \(\frac{5}{3}\) for the infinite total \(- \frac{2}{3}\).

examples.title: Keep the limiting value of a non-vanishing boundary
examples.question: Let \(F(r)=3 + \frac{4}{r + 4}\). Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}F(r+1)-F(r)\).
solution: The finite sum is \(F(n+1)-F(1)\).
The upper term tends to \(3\), not to zero.
Subtract \(\frac{19}{5}\) for the infinite total \(- \frac{4}{5}\).

examples.title: Check the degenerate geometric endpoint separately
examples.question: For real \(q\) let \(u_r=q^r-q^{r+1}\). Give all values of \(q\) for which the series converges and give the infinite sum when \(q=\frac{1}{2}\).
solution: The partial sum is \(q-q^{n+1}\). When \(|q|<1\) it tends to \(q\).
At \(q=1\) every term is zero, so it also converges. At \(q=-1\) the partial sums oscillate. For \(|q|>1\) their magnitudes grow without bound.
Thus the parameter interval is \(-1

examples.title: Find a scaled limit of a block with moving endpoints
examples.question: Let \(u_r=\frac{3}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right)}\). Find \(\lim_{n\to\infty}n\sum_{r=2 n + 1}^{4 n}u_r\).
solution: The block telescopes to \(\frac{3}{2 n + 3}\) minus \(\frac{3}{4 n + 3}\). Both terms tend to zero by themselves.
Multiply by \(n\) before taking limits. Divide each denominator by \(n\).
The result tends to \(\frac{3}{2}\) minus \(\frac{3}{4}\), so the limit is \(\frac{3}{4}\).

examples.title: Find a scaled limit of a block with moving endpoints
examples.question: Let \(u_r=\frac{5}{\left(r + 4\right) \left(r + 5\right)}\). Find \(\lim_{n\to\infty}n\sum_{r=4 n + 1}^{6 n}u_r\).
solution: The block telescopes to \(\frac{5}{4 n + 5}\) minus \(\frac{5}{6 n + 5}\). Both terms tend to zero by themselves.
Multiply by \(n\) before taking limits. Divide each denominator by \(n\).
The result tends to \(\frac{5}{4}\) minus \(\frac{5}{6}\), so the limit is \(\frac{5}{12}\).

extraPractice.prompt: Find the sum to infinity of \(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{5}{\left(r + 4\right) \left(r + 5\right)}\) and the exact error after the first \(7\) terms.
extraPractice.hint: Keep the finite boundary until you have written the exact error.
extraPractice.solution:

The final reciprocal tends to zero. This leaves \(S_\infty=1\).

Subtracting \(S_n\) from this level gives \(\frac{5}{n + 5}\). At \(7\) terms the error is \(\frac{5}{12}\).

extraPractice.prompt: For the partial sums \(S_n=1 - \frac{5}{n + 5}\), find the least positive integer \(n\) for which the difference from the limit is strictly less than \(\frac{5}{16}\).
extraPractice.hint: An integer giving exact equality does not satisfy a strict inequality.

The limit is \(1\). The positive error is \(\frac{5}{n + 5}\).

At \(n=11\) the error equals the stated tolerance. The error then decreases strictly.

Equality is excluded, so the first accepted integer is \(12\).

extraPractice.hint: Take the limit of the entire boundary term, including any constant part.
extraPractice.solution:
The finite sum is \(F(n+1)-F(1)\).

The upper term tends to \(5\), not to zero.

Subtract \(\frac{41}{7}\) for the infinite total \(- \frac{6}{7}\).

extraPractice.title: Check the degenerate geometric endpoint separately
extraPractice.prompt: For real \(q\) let \(u_r=q^r-q^{r+1}\). Give all values of \(q\) for which the series converges and give the infinite sum when \(q=\frac{2}{3}\).

extraPractice.title: Find a scaled limit of a block with moving endpoints
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(u_r=\frac{7}{\left(r + 6\right) \left(r + 7\right)}\). Find \(\lim_{n\to\infty}n\sum_{r=6 n + 1}^{8 n}u_r\).
extraPractice.hint: Determine the power of n in each boundary before taking the limit.
extraPractice.solution:
The block telescopes to \(\frac{7}{6 n + 7}\) minus \(\frac{7}{8 n + 7}\). Both terms tend to zero by themselves.

Multiply by \(n\) before taking limits. Divide each denominator by \(n\).

The result tends to \(\frac{7}{6}\) minus \(\frac{7}{8}\), so the limit is \(\frac{7}{24}\).

If \(S_n=2-\frac1{n+1}\), find its limit and the least n giving an error strictly below \(\frac{1}{5}\).

Check The limit is two. The error equals the tolerance at \(n=4\) and first falls below it at \(n=5\).
revision.checks:
• Taking a limit of the summand answers a different question from taking a limit of the sum.
  • If equality occurs at an integer and the bound is strict, the next integer is the first candidate.
